title: Wayfinding in Healthcare Facilities: Contributions from Environmental Psychology
review_question: To highlight the pivotal role of wayfinding in healthcare facilities and review advances in wayfinding research, particularly in healthcare environments, covering plan configuration, manifest cues, technology, and user characteristics.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not specified; the review synthesizes research from environmental psychology and related fields relevant to wayfinding in healthcare settings.

findings.quote: Plan configuration has an impact on wayfinding; judged simplicity is correlated to ease of wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Plan configuration (symmetry and repetition of similar elements)
findings.quote: At the same time, symmetry and repetition may lead to confusion
distinctive landmarks emerge as an aid to lessen disorientation.
Both environmental affordances (what the layout affords or makes possible) and manifest cues (signage) support wayfinding.
Building verticality (stacked floors) also present challenges to wayfinding

findings.consequent: Perceptual access and frame of reference (in multi-level buildings)
findings.quote: architectural features (e.g., a glass atrium) may provide needed perceptual access.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding difficulty (for individuals with cognitive challenges)
findings.quote: Individuals with cognitive challenges have particular difficulty with repetitive elements and information clutter.
Wayfinding for the elderly may be enhanced with more salient landmarks.

findings.antecedent: New technologies (virtual reality, space syntax, head-mounted displays, location sensing devices, mobile devices for blind users, optical character recognition, personalized accessibility maps)
findings.consequent: Advances in wayfinding research and technical support for independent wayfinding
findings.quote: A range of new technologies provides advances in research on wayfinding, joining experimental control with ecological validity.

findings.antecedent: Posted emergency signs (in virtual reality environment)
findings.quote: demonstrated a significant improvement overall in emergency egress speed when signs were posted
The authors suggest ways to reduce the cognitive load that misaligned configurations create, including the use of a vista and outside landscaping to help provide a global frame of reference.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with higher integration (more connected to other spaces)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding success (visitor behavior in public areas, especially when uncertain)
findings.quote: the importance of highly connected spaces) and provide technical support for independent wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) showing real-time location on floor plan
findings.consequent: Cognitive map formation and navigation performance (course completion time, distance traveled, navigation errors) for first responders
findings.quote: first responders using these HMDs (integrated into firefighters' masks) formed better cognitive maps than did those without the HMDs.

findings.antecedent: Mobile applications (e.g., MyWay) providing hospital maps and turn-by-turn directions
findings.quote: Mobile technologies may support patient satisfaction through improved wayfinding experiences in complex hospital settings.
Research points to differences in memory capacity for older vs. younger users, which in turn points to the need for universal design considerations for every user.

findings.antecedent: User characteristics (cognitive and sensory limitations, especially visual impairments)
findings.quote: Wayfinding research has focused on those with challenges including cognitive and sensory limitations, with a particular emphasis on those with limitations of vision.

findings.antecedent: Environmental features (lighting too bright/dim, highly reflective decorative elements, signage size/placement)
findings.quote: Lessons learned from such research (e.g., drawbacks to lighting that is too bright or dim; highly reflective decorative elements; size and placement of signage) again point to the need for universal design considerations.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding strategy (reliance on route learning over configurational knowledge) and learning rate
findings.quote: VR research with Down syndrome individuals points to a reliance on routes and the absence of configurational knowledge.

findings.consequent: Flexibility in wayfinding (switching from egocentric to allocentric perspectives) and safety issues in emergency situations
findings.quote: Similarly, older individuals have difficulty switching from egocentric to allocentric perspectives; this lack of flexibility points to safety issues in emergency situations when main routes may be blocked.

findings.antecedent: Universal healthcare symbols (abstract vs. human form)
findings.quote: This project (Hablamos Juntos or “we speak together") has met with some success, but there are limitations in the perception of abstract symbols.

findings.antecedent: Universal healthcare symbols based on the human form performing a specific action (e.g., surgery pictogram with figure, scalpel in hand)
findings.quote: Those symbols based on the human form performing a specific action (e.g., a surgery pictogram with a figure, scalpel in hand) have been more widely understood.

synthesis_conclusions: Plan configuration and manifest cues have a significant impact on wayfinding, with a tension between the need for regular environments and the importance of distinctiveness.
Virtual reality and mobile applications are increasingly important tools for both wayfinding research and practical wayfinding aids.
Research on wayfinding for individuals with cognitive and visual impairments is crucial, especially given the aging population, and highlights the need for universal design.

The development of universal healthcare symbols has shown mixed success, with abstract symbols being less understood cross-culturally compared to those depicting human forms performing specific actions.
evidence_gaps: More controlled research is needed using emerging technologies like virtual reality and mobile applications to understand their impact on wayfinding.
Further research is needed on how wayfinding in healthcare environments is affected by cognitive and visual impairments, especially with an aging population.

The search for universal healthcare symbols requires further study, as current symbols developed through projects like Hablamos Juntos still show considerable misunderstanding, particularly for abstract representations and across diverse cultures.
limitations: The review does not specify a systematic search methodology or inclusion/exclusion criteria, which is typical for a narrative review.
The review primarily synthesizes existing findings without conducting new analyses or quantitative pooling of effects.

paper_metadata.title: Wayfinding in Healthcare Facilities: Contributions from Environmental Psychology
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Wayfinding in Healthcare Facilities: Contributions from Environmental Psychology
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The ability to successfully navigate in healthcare facilities is an important goal for patients, visitors, and staff. Despite the fundamental nature of such behavior, it is not infrequent for planners to consider wayfinding only after the fact, once the building or building complex is complete. This review argues that more recognition is needed for the pivotal role of wayfinding in healthcare facilities. First, to provide context, the review presents a brief overview of the relationship between environmental psychology and healthcare facility design. Then, the core of the article covers advances in wayfinding research with an emphasis on healthcare environments, including the roles of plan configuration and manifest cues, technology, and user characteristics. Plan configuration and manifest cues, which appeared early on in wayfinding research, continue to play a role in wayfinding success and should inform design decisions. Such considerations are joined by emerging technologies (e.g., mobile applications, virtual reality, and computational models of wayfinding) as a way to both enhance our theoretical knowledge of wayfinding and advance its applications for users. Among the users discussed here are those with cognitive and/or visual challenges (e.g., Down syndrome, age-related decrements such as dementia, and limitations of vision). In addition, research on the role of cross-cultural comprehension and the effort to develop a system of universal healthcare symbols is included. The article concludes with a summary of the status of these advances and directions for future research.

environmental_features: Spatial layout complexity (e.g., grid vs. radial)
Natural light and views to nature

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Individuals form mental representations (cognitive maps) of their environment to navigate, and the quality and legibility of these maps are crucial for wayfinding success.
Wayfinding involves processing environmental cues and information, where the clarity and organization of these cues directly impact navigational decision-making.
Stressors inherent in healthcare environments can impair cognitive functions, including spatial orientation and the ability to form and use cognitive maps for wayfinding.

mechanism_chain.description: A simple and legible plan configuration reduces the cognitive effort required to process environmental information, thereby facilitating the formation of clear cognitive maps and ultimately enhancing the ease of wayfinding.

steps.to_construct: Perceived clarity and ease of understanding the spatial layout

steps.to_construct: Reduced cognitive load and improved formation of accurate cognitive maps

steps.to_construct: Increased ease of wayfinding and reduced navigational errors
